intro: From B1’s “I can express myself” to B2’s “I can argue, report and persuade”, in four phases: first make complex sentences and moods precise, then work on mediation and text organisation, then train on both the old and new DELF B2 formats task by task, and finally sit mock exams, repair what they reveal and bridge to DALF C1.

parts: Authentic radio-type documents. Two formats are in use at the same time: a long document heard twice + short documents heard only once; questions follow the order of the document and the first one tests overall understanding.

An informative article and an argumentative article (the new format also has short-document questions). The two exercises are independent and can be done in any order; read the questions before the text.
An argumentative text of at least 250 words: a forum contribution or a formal letter (in your own name or on behalf of a group), with an introduction, development and conclusion.
① Monologue: draw out the topic and the problématique of a short document, announce your outline and give a reasoned opinion; ② debate with the examiner: hold your ground, refine, concede, rebut.
exam.rule: Each paper is marked out of 25, 100 in total; you pass with 50, provided no paper scores below 5.

writing: Genre and topic as required; ≥250 words; facts set out in detail with concrete examples; a clear position, developed arguments, pros and cons weighed.
Paragraphs (introduction – development – conclusion); punctuation that helps understanding; layout suited to the genre; varied connectors organising the ideas.
Appropriate forms of address and politeness; register suited to the situation.
B2-level vocabulary suited to the situation; synonyms to avoid repetition; precise word choice, spelling mostly correct.
A mix of simple and complex sentences; past tenses, conditional and subjunctive used correctly; accurate gender and number agreement.
speaking: Draw out the document’s topic and main ideas; state a clear problématique; announce an outline; argue with relevant examples; have an opening and a close, with varied connectors.
Confirm and refine opinions; concede with cependant / toutefois / malgré; agree or disagree; respond to the examiner and defend a position.
B2 vocabulary with little repetition; simple and complex sentences; correct tenses and agreement; self-correction; clear pronunciation, moderate pace, varied intonation.

listening: Before listening, read the questions and try to remember them; they follow the order of the recording, and the first tests overall understanding.
Note: long documents are heard twice, short ones only once — with a short document, lock onto the speaker’s position from the start.
First listening: note the key points — type of document, topic, main idea and keywords.
Pay special attention to each speaker’s position, attitude and tone (approval, reservation, irony).
If you don’t understand a word, infer the overall meaning from the context.
reading: The two exercises are independent and can be done in any order; 1 hour goes fast, so plan your time.
For each exercise, read the questions first, then the text; the first question tests the overall meaning and questions follow the order of the text.
As you read, underline the topic, main idea and keywords — especially concessions, contrasts and the author’s evaluative words.
Tell facts from opinions: the author’s real position often comes after pourtant, toutefois, en revanche.
writing: Read the instructions and the prompt document carefully: topic, genre (forum post / formal letter), keywords, the view you must respond to.
Outline on scrap paper: introduction (context + question + position) — 2 to 3 argument paragraphs (point + explanation + example) — conclusion.
Give each argument a concrete example, and deal with one opposing view (Certes…, mais…).
Keep 5 minutes to check spelling, agreement and moods; write the word count at the end (≥250 words).
speaking: 30 minutes’ preparation: pick one of two topics; underline the document’s keywords, write only an outline, not full sentences, and anticipate the examiner’s questions.
Monologue: state the document’s topic → raise the problématique → announce the outline → argue with examples → conclude.
Debate: confirm and refine your position, concede (certes, cependant, malgré), respond to the examiner and defend your view.
Look at the examiner as you speak; articulate clearly at a moderate pace; correct yourself when you slip.
